title: Già hóa dân số và tuổi nghỉ hưu · Agree / Disagree
prompt: Some people believe that raising the retirement age as life expectancy increases should be a priority. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

grammar.name: Đối lập hai mệnh đề
grammar.example: Longer lives increase pension costs, but the ability to work longer depends on health and occupation rather than the national average lifespan alone.
grammar.why: Trong câu mở, but nối lợi ích dự kiến với giới hạn thực hiện cụ thể. Mở bài nêu đúng mối nối tài chính giữa tuổi thọ và hưu trí, đồng thời tách khả năng làm việc của cá nhân khỏi chỉ số trung bình để tránh suy luận từ dân số sang mọi nghề.

paragraphs: Longer lives increase pension costs, but the ability to work longer depends on health and occupation rather than the national average lifespan alone. I support later retirement for people able to continue working, alongside earlier access for demanding occupations and a practical option of gradual retirement.

Later retirement can ease pressure on public pension systems. Longer contribution periods help finance longer lives without placing the entire burden on younger workers. An employee in a flexible advisory role might continue working part-time. Part-time continuation can preserve expertise and contributions without demanding the same workload, illustrating why flexible exit may be preferable to a single abrupt threshold. An increase in average life expectancy does not mean that a construction worker and an office adviser can safely extend their careers by the same number of years.

Healthy life expectancy and physical demands differ sharply between occupations. Longer average lives can conceal large differences in years of good health. Requiring physically demanding work to continue on the same terms as desk-based employment may shift pension savings onto people least able to extend their working lives safely. Earlier access for demanding occupations needs clear eligibility, while gradual retirement should remain a practical option rather than depend entirely on individual employers' goodwill. Eligibility for earlier pensions should reflect documented occupational demands, while part-time transitions let healthier employees reduce workloads without losing their entire earned income at once. Pension reform should balance contribution periods with healthy life expectancy and occupational demands, rather than use longevity alone to justify a uniform retirement age.
Pension sustainability requires longer contributions from those who can manage them, together with protection for workers whose health makes an equally long career unrealistic.
